title: Signs Revised Travel Ban Executive Order
description_short: Signed Executive Order 13780 revising the travel ban and suspending entry from several countries.
description_medium: On March 6, 2017, Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his first travel-ban order after courts blocked it. The revised order suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, while excluding Iraq and providing exceptions. It also paused refugee admissions for 120 days, subject to waivers, and prompted further legal challenges.
description_long: Executive Order 13780, signed March 6, 2017, replaced the January travel order after federal courts blocked key parts of the earlier version. It suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of six countries—Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen—while removing Iraq from the earlier list. The order included exceptions for lawful permanent residents, people with valid visas and certain other cases, and authorized case-by-case waivers. Separately, it paused decisions and travel under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for 120 days, also with exceptions, while agencies reviewed screening procedures. The order set a 50,000-person ceiling for refugee admissions in fiscal year 2017. Its effective date was March 16, and opponents again challenged it in court. The administration described the restrictions as a national-security measure; critics argued that the policy continued to target predominantly Muslim countries. The order’s national-origin restrictions and refugee pause were legally contested and later superseded by subsequent travel restrictions. This account describes what the revised order directed and the immediate dispute; it does not treat the government’s security rationale as an independently established finding.

preserved_fields.title: Signs Revised Travel Ban Executive Order
preserved_fields.description_short: Signed Executive Order 13780 revising the travel ban and suspending entry from several countries.

notes: The Federal Register text of EO 13780 identifies the six countries, 90-day entry suspension and 120-day refugee pause; the New York Times published the order text and identified it as signed March 6. Iraq was removed from the original list. The supplied White House link is to the January order, so the Federal Register is the operative text used here.

title: Trump Turns White House Ballroom into a 'Military Complex'
description_short: Trump Turns White House Ballroom into a 'Military Complex'
description_medium: In August 2026, the Trump administration defended construction of a White House ballroom as a national-security facility after courts challenged the project’s authorization. A court order required above-ground ballroom construction to stop unless Congress acted. An administration filing described proposed blast- and missile-resistant features, intensifying the dispute over the project’s purpose and legal basis.
description_long: The White House ballroom project became the subject of a legal fight over both congressional authorization and the administration’s explanation for the construction. The Independent reported in August 2026 that Trump officials increasingly described the planned venue as a national-security structure, after initially promoting it as a space for events. A federal appeals court had ordered the government to stop ballroom construction by August 21 unless Congress authorized it. In a court filing, the administration listed claimed security features, including blast-resistant glass, reinforced columns, a drone-resistant roof, military-grade ventilation and underground facilities. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued to stop the project, said courts had allowed underground security work to continue but had blocked the above-ground ballroom absent proper authorization. The administration argued that the venue would protect the president and other officials; the court dispute had not established that the full ballroom was legally authorized. The episode illustrates how national-security claims became part of the administration’s defense of a major construction project at the White House. “Military complex” was the report’s characterization of that shift, not a formal designation of the building.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Turns White House Ballroom into a 'Military Complex'
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Turns White House Ballroom into a 'Military Complex'

notes: The Independent reports the August 21 stop-construction deadline and quotes the administration filing’s security specifications; it also describes the National Trust’s position and the courts’ distinction between underground security work and the above-ground ballroom. The phrase “military complex” is journalistic framing.

title: Trump Sued Over Selling Early Access to Truth Social Posts
description_short: Trump Sued Over Selling Early Access to Truth Social Posts
description_medium: A federal lawsuit has been filed against President Donald Trump, accusing him of violating the First Amendment by selling special advance access to his Truth Social posts. The lawsuit claims that this practice is unconstitutional and gives certain individuals unfair access to the president's thoughts and ideas.
description_long: The lawsuit described in the preserved medium was filed in federal court on August 12, 2026, by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept. It challenged Truth API, a paid service connected to Truth Social that offered subscribers early access to posts by Trump and other government officials. The service was reported to cost as much as $100,000 per month, with a lower monthly price for a multiyear commitment. The plaintiffs argued that giving paying customers advance access to official announcements while restricting other publishers’ ability to collect the posts violated the First and Fifth Amendments. They said the arrangement disadvantaged news organizations that relied on timely access and could undermine equal access to presidential statements. The suit named Trump and White House social-media staff and asked a federal court to stop them from carrying out the access restrictions. These are allegations in a complaint, not a court ruling that the service is unconstitutional. At filing, the dispute concerned both the fee-based early-access product and efforts to prevent automated collection of public posts. The legal outcome remained unresolved in the reporting reviewed.
organization_tags: Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington

title: Finalizes “Secret Science” Rule
description_short: EPA finalized a rule restricting use of certain scientific studies in rulemaking, weakening environmental protections.
description_medium: On January 5, 2021, the EPA finalized its “Strengthening Transparency in Regulatory Science” rule, which gave greater weight to studies whose underlying dose-response data were available for independent validation. The agency said it would protect personal and confidential business information. Critics warned the standard could limit regulators’ use of important public-health studies.
description_long: The EPA finalized the rule on January 5, 2021, near the end of the Trump administration. It directed the agency to give greater consideration to studies whose underlying dose-response data could be independently validated when developing influential scientific information or significant regulations. The EPA said the rule would not require publication of personally identifiable or confidential business information and established peer-review requirements for pivotal science. Supporters described the change as a transparency measure. Public-health researchers and environmental advocates warned that the data-access standard could make influential studies harder to use when confidentiality rules prevent the release of individual-level information. That concern mattered because epidemiological studies had informed regulations addressing air pollution and toxic substances. The rule did not prohibit EPA from considering all research lacking public raw data, but its criteria changed how the agency would weigh some studies in consequential decisions. The rule’s scope and effect became a subject of dispute; reporting described it as a final Trump-era rollback, while the agency presented it as a way to strengthen validation and preserve privacy. The record concerns the rule’s finalization, not a claim that the underlying scientific studies were invalid.
subcategory: Scientific Research Suppression and Researcher Persecution

preserved_fields.title: Finalizes “Secret Science” Rule
preserved_fields.description_short: EPA finalized a rule restricting use of certain scientific studies in rulemaking, weakening environmental protections.
preserved_fields.subcategory: Scientific Research Suppression and Researcher Persecution

notes: EPA’s January 5 release says the rule prioritized dose-response studies with data available for independent validation and protected personally identifiable and confidential business information. AP and the Washington Post report critics’ concern that restrictions could make key public-health studies less usable. The original linked EPA endpoint was unavailable; these sources provide the rule’s text and its contested context.

title: House Committee Releases Trump Tax Returns
description_short: The House Ways and Means Committee released six years of Trump’s tax returns after a long legal fight.
description_medium: On December 30, 2022, the House Ways and Means Committee released redacted federal tax returns for Donald and Melania Trump and Trump business entities covering 2015–2020. The disclosure followed years of litigation. A separate committee report found the IRS had delayed required presidential audits, including beginning the audit of Trump’s 2016 return only in 2019.
description_long: The House Ways and Means Committee released thousands of pages of redacted returns for Donald and Melania Trump and several Trump business entities on December 30, 2022. The records covered tax years 2015 through 2020 and followed a legal fight that reached the Supreme Court, which cleared the way for the Treasury Department to provide the returns to the committee. The committee said it sought them to examine the IRS program requiring annual audits of presidential returns. In a separate report, the Democratic majority found that the IRS had not timely carried out that requirement during Trump’s presidency: the audit of his 2016 return began on April 3, 2019, after the committee requested information, and was not complete when he left office. The released returns also showed years in which Trump reported negative income and comparatively low federal income-tax payments, though the committee’s accompanying analysis and the raw returns were distinct records. The release did not itself determine whether any tax return was unlawful. It made previously private filings available for public review and exposed questions about IRS oversight and the process for auditing a sitting president.

preserved_fields.title: House Committee Releases Trump Tax Returns
preserved_fields.description_short: The House Ways and Means Committee released six years of Trump’s tax returns after a long legal fight.

notes: NBC, Reuters and AP report the release of returns for 2015–2020 after litigation. NBC and AP report the committee’s separate finding that the IRS began the mandatory 2016 audit in April 2019 and had not completed it by the end of Trump’s term. The returns and the committee’s audit report are distinct records.
